name: Funazushi (Shiga fermented crucian carp sushi)
text: A fermented sushi of Lake Biwa nigorobuna that is described as the oldest surviving form of sushi, tied to the Omi region. The fish are scaled and gutted with the roe left intact, salt-cured (called shiokiri in Shiga), washed, then layered with salted cooked rice in a tub under a weight and left to ferment through several months, traditionally until the New Year. Sources give a wide ripening range, roughly half a year to two years.
flavor: Fermented, sour and salty; the rice acts as the fermenting medium and the fish is the part eaten.
use: Sliced thin to bite size and served as an accompaniment to sake; a home version is described using shio-kiri fish sold by the fishermen's federation.
craft: Key stages in the sources: salt-cure the gutted fish (roe kept unbroken), rinse off residual viscera and drain well, then pack in a tub alternating fish and rice, with the rice seasoned to about onigiri saltiness, and press under a heavy stone. Judge by the length of the ferment, since producers differ from months to two years; do not treat a single duration as standard.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Funazushi (Shiga)

name: Kyo yudofu (Kyoto simmered tofu)
text: Tofu gently heated in a pot of hot water or kombu liquid and eaten with dipping sauce. Kyoto's tradition is tied to its good groundwater, which supported tofu making for centuries, and to Zen temple shojin cuisine. The popular account says it began at the tea houses at the gate of Nanzen-ji, but other sources state there is no document or record supporting a Nanzen-ji origin. It spread among ordinary people from the Edo period.
flavor: Clean, soft and delicate; the flavor comes from the soybean and from the dipping sauce rather than from the broth.
use: A winter pot dish in Kyoto, with a Kyoto-style version adding mizuna (kyona), a winter vegetable grown mainly around Kyoto.
craft: The attribution to Nanzen-ji is a tradition, not a documented fact; say so on a menu rather than assert it. The pitfall in any tofu pot is overheating, which toughens the tofu; the sources stress the water quality that underlies Kyoto tofu.

name: Obanzai (Kyoto home-style side dishes)
text: The term for the everyday side dishes cooked in ordinary Kyoto households. The word became widely known only relatively recently: one source credits the cooking writer Doi Katsu and others with popularizing it in the 1960s while introducing Kyoto home cooking. Kyoto vegetables (kyo-yasai) are central, and the MAFF regional cuisine pages for Kyoto place vegetable-based side dishes at the heart of the local food culture.
flavor: Plain, seasonal, vegetable-led home cooking.
use: Served as small dishes of simmered or dressed seasonal vegetables, often several at once, in homes and in restaurants that cook in that style.
craft: Treat obanzai as a household category, not a fixed recipe list; the term's wide use is a modern one, so avoid claims of an ancient codified repertoire.

name: Kushikatsu (Osaka skewered cutlets)
text: Skewered, breaded and deep-fried morsels dipped in a shared sauce, tied to the Shinsekai district of Osaka. The origin is disputed: one account says a Shinsekai restaurateur devised it as cheap, filling food for workers with short breaks, while a Toyo Keizai article argues it came to Osaka from Tokyo stall culture and names Umeda's Nikatsu Tokyoya. The long-established shop Daruma, founded in 1929, is cited as the source of the 'no double-dipping' sauce rule and the fine-crumbed batter style.
flavor: Crisp fine coating; eaten with a shared, thin Worcester-style sauce.
use: Dipped once in the communal sauce; the double-dip ban is explained as hygiene, because saliva would enter the shared sauce.
craft: Sources attribute the Osaka style to a fine-grained coating; the dip-once rule is a service point a professional must design around, for example by offering a cabbage scoop for extra sauce rather than re-dipping.

name: Kasu-udon (Osaka aburakasu udon)
text: Udon in a hot dashi soup topped with aburakasu, the crisped residue of rendered beef or pork offal fat that is classed as a type of horumon. It is distinct from tenkasu udon, which uses tempura crumbs. In the home method described, the aburakasu is sliced to about 2 mm, added once the soup is hot so that its white fat melts into it, and the heat is turned off. Sources found did not establish its history in Osaka.
flavor: Rich, fat-forward soup; the melted aburakasu gives savory depth.
use: Served as a hot noodle dish in a udon tsuyu base with the sliced aburakasu dissolved in the soup.
craft: Slice thin (about 2 mm), add after boiling the udon and heating the soup, stop heating when the fat melts. Do not confuse aburakasu with tempura scraps; the two give entirely different dishes.
src: HugKum: kasu-udon explained with home recipe

name: Botan-nabe (Tanba-Sasayama wild boar pot)
text: A wild boar (inoshishi) hot pot of Hyogo, centered on Tanba-Sasayama. The prefecture's description is a dashi broth based on a blend of white and red miso with boar meat and seasonal vegetables. The MAFF recipe is provided by the Izumi-kai of Tanba-Sasayama city, and it is eaten with ground sansho pepper sprinkled on.
flavor: Miso-rich, with the strong flavor of boar meat balanced by seasonal vegetables and sansho.
use: Cold-season communal pot; finish at the table with powdered sansho.
craft: The base is a white and red miso blend in dashi, so balance the two misos against the boar's fat. Source detail on slicing and timing was not available, so confirm those with the local producer.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Botan-nabe (Hyogo)

name: Ikanago no kugi-ni (simmered sand lance)
text: Small ikanago (sand lance) simmered in soy sauce, sugar and ginger into a sweet-savory tsukudani-style preserve. The name comes from the finished fish, which curl and resemble rusted nails (kugi). It is listed among Hyogo's regional dishes by the Kinki agricultural bureau. In Mie Prefecture the equivalent dish, made from kounago, is named for the same reason: the slender fish bend when simmered and look like rusted nails.
flavor: Sweet and salty with ginger.
use: A rice accompaniment and gift preserve.
craft: The core seasoning in the sources is soy sauce, sugar and ginger. The sources do not give ratios or timings, so state ratios from your own tests, not these references.

name: Kakinoha-zushi (persimmon-leaf sushi)
text: Slices of salt-cured mackerel pressed onto small portions of vinegared rice and wrapped in persimmon leaves, associated with Gojo and the Yoshino area of Nara. MAFF notes that its beginnings are uncertain, with accounts pointing to the Nanboku-cho period or the 1800s, and that it was originally a vinegar-free narezushi. Mackerel, salt and rice arrived from afar and were precious, so it was a festival and celebration food; the present form is said to date from railway-era station kiosk sales. Nara and Wakayama also use sea bream, conger and shiitake.
flavor: Vinegared rice with firmly salted mackerel, wrapped in leaf.
use: Festival and celebration dish, now sold widely as a packaged sushi.
craft: MAFF method: thin skin is peeled from the salt-cured mackerel, which is sliced thin; vinegared rice is pressed in a mold, portioned, topped with fish and wrapped in the leaf. One account says Kishu fishermen carried salted mackerel over passes to riverside villages along the Yoshino River, but the birthplace is not settled.

name: Mehari-zushi (Kumano wrapped rice balls)
text: Large rice balls wrapped in salt-pickled takana (mustard greens) leaves, from the southern part of Wakayama where fishing and forestry are the main industries. It spread as a quick lunch eaten between busy fishing or mountain work. The MAFF home recipe for two to three people uses 2 go of rice, 5 leaves of salted takana and a seasoning of 1 tbsp soy sauce with 1/2 tsp mirin to taste.
flavor: Salty pickled-leaf wrapper around plain rice.
use: Eaten out of hand as a worker's lunch; the name is explained either as opening the mouth wide, as if the eyes widen, or as being so delicious that you open your eyes wide.
craft: Rinse and squeeze the takana, season it with the soy and mirin, cook the rice, use the minced leaf stem as a core, then wrap with the leaf and shape. Keep the leaf seasoning light since the pickle is already salty.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Mehari-zushi (Wakayama)

name: Igisu (Tottori egonori jelly)
text: A set jelly made from igisu-so, a seaweed also called egonori. It is said to have been offered to the court in the Asuka and Nara periods. The dried weed is washed and rehydrated, boiled in a pot until dissolved, then set; it is eaten with vinegared miso or soy sauce. It is often served at Buddhist vegetarian meals, festivals, and weddings and funerals.
flavor: Cool, firm jelly taken with the sharp-sweet vinegar miso or soy.
use: Cut from the set block and served with su-miso or soy sauce at ceremonial meals.
craft: The set depends on fully dissolving the dried weed, so simmer until no fibers remain; the sources give no ratios or times, so test your setting strength against the specific lot of weed.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Igisu (Tottori)

name: Shijimi-jiru (Shinji-ko clam miso soup)
text: A soup of yamato-shijimi from Lake Shinji, which MAFF notes yields one of the top catches in Japan with large clams, and which has long been an everyday dish in the Izumo region. The preparation point stressed in the source is to let the clams spit sand overnight in water of about the same salinity as their habitat.
flavor: Savory clam broth.
use: Daily soup in the Izumo area.
craft: Soak the shijimi overnight in water matching the salinity of the lake rather than in fresh water, so the clams stay alive and release their sand. The source summary does not give the miso or time details.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Shijimi-jiru (Shimane)

name: Okayama barazushi (matsuri-zushi)
ja: 岡山ばらずし（まつりずし）
text: Scattered sushi of the Bizen Okayama area, also called matsuri-zushi or Bizen barazushi, made for festivals, celebrations and to entertain guests. A frequently told origin is that the domain lord Ikeda Mitsumasa issued a frugality decree, so the common people mixed fish and vegetables into the sushi rice rather than serve several side dishes. The topping set follows the season, with Spanish mackerel (sawara) in spring and matsutake in autumn.
flavor: Sweet-sour rice with seasonal fish and vegetables mixed in.
use: Festival and guest dish; the ingredients change with the season.
craft: Fit the topping to the season (sawara in spring, matsutake in autumn per MAFF). The Ikeda Mitsumasa story is a traditional account, so present it as such.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Matsuri-zushi/Barazushi (Okayama)

name: Kaki no dote-nabe (Hiroshima oyster pot)
text: A Hiroshima oyster pot in which miso is spread in a bank around the inside of the pot. The Hiroshima page on MAFF's site says the name has three explanations, one being that the miso is plastered up the pot's inner wall like an embankment (dote). Hiroshima is the largest oyster-producing prefecture, and shell mounds show wild oysters were eaten in the Jomon and Yayoi periods.
flavor: Oysters cooked against a miso bank that dissolves slowly into the broth.
use: A cold-season pot of oysters and vegetables.
craft: The distinguishing technique is the miso embankment, which melts gradually into the broth as it cooks. Detailed amounts and the other two name explanations are on the individual MAFF page.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Hiroshima prefecture

name: Kaki-meshi (Hiroshima oyster rice)
text: Oyster takikomi rice that arose around Etajima, where oyster farming is active. The main ingredients listed by MAFF are oysters, rice, carrot, burdock, dried shiitake and aburaage. Hiroshima is the top oyster producer in Japan.
flavor: Oyster and burdock savoriness through the rice.
use: Home dish in the oyster season.
craft: The source gives the ingredient list but not the timing. Oysters shrink and toughen with overcooking, so confirm your add-in timing against your own tests.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Kaki-meshi (Hiroshima)

name: Kawara soba (Kawatana roof-tile soba)
text: Cha-soba (green tea buckwheat noodles) served on a heated roof tile, topped with shredded egg omelet (kinshi-tamago) and beef, eaten dipped in mentsuyu. MAFF dates its creation to 1961 (Showa 36), and the area of transmission is Kawatana Onsen.
flavor: Crisped noodle underside from the hot tile, with egg and beef; dipped in tsuyu.
use: Served on the tile at the table and dipped in sauce.
craft: The tile is the cooking surface, so heat control matters; the source summary gives no tile temperature or timing.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Kawara soba (Yamaguchi)

name: Kencho (Yamaguchi simmered tofu and root vegetables)
text: A Yamaguchi home dish of tofu, daikon and carrot simmered together, with a sweet-salty, somewhat strong seasoning that suits rice. It is listed in MAFF's Yamaguchi section with a step-by-step recipe.
flavor: Sweet-savory, a little strong.
use: A home side dish eaten with rice.
craft: Seasoning is on the sweet and strong side by design, so adjust for use in a course. The source summary offers no precise ratios.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Kencho (Yamaguchi)

name: Soba-gome jiru (Iya buckwheat groat soup)
text: A Tokushima soup of soba-gome, buckwheat groats prepared by boiling the grain in salted water and drying it, simmered with vegetables and meat in dashi. MAFF names the Iya area of Miyoshi city and the whole prefecture as the areas of transmission. The listed ingredients for four people include 120 g of soba-gome, chicken thigh, carrot, dried shiitake, konnyaku, chikuwa and green onion.
flavor: Soft, grain-like groats in a savory dashi.
use: A hearty soup or zosui.
craft: MAFF prep: boil the soba-gome in eight times its volume of water for 10 to 15 minutes, rinse and drain in a sieve before adding it to the soup.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Soba-gome zosui / jiru (Tokushima)

name: Iriko-meshi (Kagawa dried-sardine rice)
text: A Kagawa takikomi rice cooked with iriko (dried small fish). The main area of transmission named by MAFF is the Seisan (western Sanuki) region, known as a producing area around Ibuki Island. Ingredients listed include rice, iriko, carrot, daikon, taro, konnyaku and aburaage.
flavor: Strong dried-fish savoriness through the rice.
use: Home dish of the iriko-producing area.
craft: Iriko carries the dashi flavor in the rice, so the quality of the iriko decides the result; the source summary gives no quantities.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Iriko-meshi (Kagawa)

name: Jakoten (Uwajima fried fish cake)
text: A fried fish cake of the Nanyo area of Ehime. MAFF records two name theories: it comes from 'zako-ten', after the small mixed fish used, or from haranbo (hotaru-jako), the raw fish. Its start is traced to 1615 (Genna 1), when Date Hidemune, the first lord of Uwajima domain, brought kamaboko craftsmen to make it.
flavor: Fried fish paste made with small whole fish.
use: Eaten as a local fish-cake dish in Nanyo.
craft: Raw material is small whole fish, per the name theories; the source summary does not provide process steps.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Jakoten (Ehime)

name: Inaka-zushi (Kochi mountain sushi)
text: A sushi from the mountain districts of Kochi that uses vegetables. MAFF says it began when kombu and nori were hard to get, so mountain ingredients were used. Main materials include myoga, ryukyu (taro-stem), konnyaku, bamboo shoots and shihochiku bamboo shoots.
flavor: Vegetable-based, with no seafood wrapper.
use: A mountain-village sushi eaten at gatherings.
craft: Seasoning and shaping details are not in the source summary. The defining point is that vegetables replace sea-derived toppings and wrappers.
src: MAFF Uchi no Kyodo Ryori: Inaka-zushi (Kochi)
